title: The Remaining Prepositions, and Reflexive Phrases
summary: The prepositions not yet given, set out with the whole system in one table; and the reflexive verbs, which at this level are learnt as set phrases rather than as a paradigm.

rules.heading: Pas: to a Person
rules.statement: **Pas** with the **accusative** means *to* or *at somebody's place*. It is used of **people only** — one goes *į Vilnių* but *pas brolį* — and it covers both the going and the being there, where English needs *to my brother's* and *at my brother's*.

examples.gloss: I am going to my mother's.
Yesterday I was at the doctor's.

footnotes: *Į* with a person is wrong: *važiuoju į mamą* would mean driving into her.

rules.heading: Per and Prieš of Place
rules.statement: ¶87 gave both of these as prepositions of **time**. Each has a use of **place** as well, and the case is the accusative in either sense. **Per** is *across* or *through*; **prieš** is *in front of*, and is the opposite of *už* (¶62).

paradigms.caption: The same word, time and place

rows.label: prieš
cells: prieš namą — in front of the house

examples.gloss: We are going across the bridge.
In front of the house there is a garden.

rules.heading: Už with the Accusative: Payment and Thanks
rules.statement: **Už** was given at ¶62 with the **genitive**, meaning *behind*. With the **accusative** it means *for* in the sense of payment or return — and it is the *už* of *ačiū už*, thank you for. It is also the *than* of ¶119. One word, three cases of meaning, and the ending decides which.

rows.label: accusative
cells: sumokėjo už darbą — he paid for the work

rows.label: accusative
cells: didesnis už mane — bigger than I

examples.gloss: How much did you pay for the ticket?

rules.heading: Virš and Vidury
rules.statement: Two more prepositions of place, both governing the **genitive**. **Virš** is *above* — not touching, and so the opposite of *ant* (¶33). **Vidury** is *in the middle of*, and is a noun in the locative pressed into service as a preposition, which is why it takes a genitive after it.

examples.gloss: The table is in the middle of the room.
The lamp hangs above the table.
examples.note: *ant stalo* would be lying on it

rules.heading: Po in a Third Sense
rules.statement: **Po** has now been met with the genitive (*after*, ¶33) and with the instrumental (*under*, ¶75). With the **accusative** it means motion **about** or **around** a place, with no particular destination — *vaikščiojome po parką*, we walked about the park. Three cases, three meanings, one word: it is the clearest demonstration in the language of why a preposition must be learnt together with its case.

examples.gloss: We walked about the town all day.

rules.heading: The Prepositions Reviewed
rules.statement: Every preposition of the level, set out by the case it governs. The genitive takes much the largest share; the accusative belongs chiefly to motion and to time; the instrumental has only two. Where a word appears twice, the **case** carries the difference in meaning, and it always does.

paradigms.caption: The whole system

rows.label: genitive
cells: ant, be, iki, nuo, prie, už, iš, po, virš, vidury

rows.label: accusative
cells: į, pas, per, prieš, už, po

paradigms.footnote: Three words govern more than one case: **už** (gen. *behind*, acc. *for, than*), **po** (gen. *after*, instr. *under*, acc. *about*), and **per** and **prieš**, which keep the accusative in both their senses.

examples.target: Nuo Kauno iki Vilniaus šimtas kilometrų.
examples.gloss: From Kaunas to Vilnius is a hundred kilometres.

rules.heading: Reflexive Verbs as Set Phrases
rules.statement: A **reflexive** verb carries the affix **-si**, which turns the action back on the doer: *mokyti* is to teach, *mokytis* to learn. The full paradigm belongs to a later level; what an A1 learner needs is to **recognise** the affix and to know a handful of phrases by heart, because several of the commonest sentences in the language are reflexive and cannot be avoided.

paradigms.caption: The phrases to know
paradigms.footnote: Note that under negation the affix **moves to the front** of the word: *mokausi* but *nesimokau*. This is the one thing about reflexives worth noticing now, because it makes a negated reflexive hard to recognise otherwise.

examples.target: Aš mokausi lietuvių kalbos, bet dar nesimokau rašyti.
examples.gloss: I am learning Lithuanian, but I am not yet learning to write.

vocabulary.gloss: to pay; to know how to

vocabulary.notes: Reflexive; under negation the -si- moves to the front: nesimoko.
Kaip sekasi? — How are you getting on?
A set phrase from the reflexive atsiprašyti.

drills.stem: Complete: **Važiuoju ____ mamą.** (I am going to my mother's.)
drills.explanation: **Pas** with the accusative is used of going to a **person**. *į* is for places; *važiuoju į mamą* would mean driving into her.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ačiū ____ kavą.** (Thank you for the coffee.)
drills.explanation: **Už** with the accusative is *for* in the sense of return or payment, and it is the *už* of thanking. With the genitive the same word would mean *behind*.
A reflexive set phrase, and one of the commonest sentences in the language. The *-si* affix is the mark of the reflexive, and here the verb is impersonal besides.

drills.stem: **Lempa kabo virš stalo.** Why *virš* and not *ant*?
options: Because *virš* is *above* without touching, while *ant* is *on*, resting upon.
Because *ant* is only used of people.
drills.explanation: Both govern the genitive; the difference is contact. *Ant stalo* would have the lamp lying on the table.

drills.stem: **Po** appears in all four. In which does it govern the **accusative**?
drills.explanation: With the accusative *po* is *about, around*. *po stalu* is instrumental (*under*) and *po pietų* genitive (*after*). Three cases, three meanings, one word.

drills.stem: Complete: **Einame ____ tiltą.** (We are going across the bridge.)
drills.explanation: **Per** with the accusative is *across* or *through* of place, as it is *within* of time. The case is the accusative in both senses.

drills.stem: **Aš mokausi, bet dar nesimokau rašyti.** What has happened to the reflexive affix in the second verb?
options: It has moved to the front of the word, after the negative.
drills.explanation: Under negation the *-si-* migrates from the end to just after *ne-*: *mokausi* but *nesimokau*. Without knowing this a learner cannot recognise a negated reflexive at all.

drills.stem: Which of these correctly pair a preposition with a case it can govern?
options: už + accusative — for, in return for
vidury + genitive — in the middle of
drills.explanation: *pas* governs the **accusative** only: *pas gydytoją*. *už* is the clearest case of one word taking two cases with two meanings, and *vidury* is a locative noun doing a preposition's work, which is why a genitive follows it.

drills.stem: Which case do **most** of the prepositions of this level govern?
drills.explanation: The genitive: *ant, be, iki, nuo, prie, už, iš, po, virš, vidury*. The accusative belongs chiefly to motion and to time, the instrumental has only *su* and *po*, and **no** preposition governs the dative at all.

drills.stem: How many different cases can **po** govern?
drills.explanation: Three: genitive for *after*, instrumental for *under*, accusative for *about, around*. It is the strongest argument in the language for learning every preposition together with its case, since the word alone tells you nothing.

drills.title: Sekmadienį po miestą
drills.passage: Sekmadienį vaikščiojome po senamiestį. Prieš katedrą laukė daug žmonių, o vidury aikštės grojo muzikantai. Ėjome per tiltą prie upės; virš vandens skraidė paukščiai. Paskui buvome pas draugą — jis gyvena virš kavinės, trečiame aukšte. „Kaip sekasi?“ — paklausė jis. „Puikiai, tik pavargau“, — atsakiau. Už kavą nemokėjome nieko: jis nieko neėmė.
drills.translation: On Sunday we walked about the old town. In front of the cathedral many people were waiting, and in the middle of the square musicians were playing. We went across the bridge by the river; birds were flying above the water. Afterwards we were at a friend's — he lives above a café, on the third floor. "How are you getting on?" he asked. "Splendidly, only I'm tired," I answered. We paid nothing for the coffee: he took nothing.

questions.explanation: *jis gyvena virš kavinės* — above the café, not touching it. *po kavine* with the instrumental would put him underneath.

questions.stem: Which prepositions in the passage govern the **accusative**?
questions.explanation: *po* here is *about, around*; *prieš* is *in front of*; *per* is *across*. All three take the accusative. *virš* governs the genitive, as *vandens* shows.

questions.stem: The last sentence contains **nieko** twice. How many negated verbs must accompany them?
questions.explanation: Two — *nemokėjome* and *neėmė*. A negative word cannot stand beside an unnegated verb (¶132), so each *nieko* brings its own *ne-*, and the genitive form is required besides, a negated verb governing the genitive (¶26).
